ne-f804d1d2.stem: Which of the following about the glossopharyngeal nerve is FALSE?
options: It stimulates parotid secretion through the otic ganglion.
It is the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
It carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue.
It carries baroreceptor information from the carotid sinus.
It carries both taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue.
ne-f804d1d2.explanation: IX carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, the pharyngeal mucosa and information from the carotid sinus and body; its only muscle is stylopharyngeus. Taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani (VII) and general sensation by the lingual nerve (V3).

ne-c4430a06.stem: When asked to say 'aah', the patient's uvula deviates to the right. Which nerve and side are affected?
ne-c4430a06.explanation: The muscles of the soft palate (levator veli palatini and others) are supplied by the vagus nerve. With one side paralysed, the healthy side pulls the palate towards itself, so the uvula deviates to the healthy side, away from the lesion. The tongue, by contrast, deviates towards the side of the lesion.

ne-bc679c52.stem: Under which structure does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hook before turning upwards?
options: Arch of the aorta (just lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum)
ne-bc679c52.explanation: The left recurrent nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta beside the ligamentum arteriosum; the right recurrent nerve turns under the right subclavian artery. Because of its long course, the left nerve can be compressed by an aortic aneurysm, an enlarged left atrium or a lung tumour, causing hoarseness.

ne-e83d1843.stem: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres?
ne-e83d1843.explanation: The cranial parasympathetic outflow travels in four nerves: III (ciliary ganglion – pupil and accommodation), VII (pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia), IX (otic ganglion – parotid) and X (thoracic and abdominal organs).

ne-a9ee3049.stem: Which is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem?
ne-a9ee3049.explanation: The trochlear fibres cross in the midbrain and emerge from the dorsal surface below the inferior colliculi. It is the thinnest cranial nerve and has the longest intracranial course. It supplies the superior oblique of the opposite side.

ne-e3ffe10b.stem: After squeezing a boil on the face a patient develops fever, periorbital oedema and proptosis; cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected. Which cranial nerve is expected to be affected first, and why?
options: Maxillary nerve; because it lies in the floor of the sinus
Oculomotor nerve; because it is highest in the lateral wall of the sinus
Optic nerve; because it passes through the sinus
Trochlear nerve; because it runs free inside the sinus
Abducens nerve; because it runs free inside the sinus together with the internal carotid artery
ne-e3ffe10b.explanation: In the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus lie, from above downwards, III, IV, V1 and V2; inside the sinus are the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve. Abducens palsy (limited lateral gaze) is therefore often the first sign. The 'danger triangle' of the face communicates with the sinus through the ophthalmic veins.

ne-eed7e04e.stem: How are the cords of the brachial plexus named?
options: By their position relative to the second part of the axillary artery
By their position relative to scalenus anterior
By their position relative to the clavicle
By the spinal segments they come from
ne-eed7e04e.explanation: The lateral, medial and posterior cords surround the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor and are named after their position relative to it. The roots (C5–T1) lie in the scalene gap, the trunks in the posterior triangle and the divisions behind the clavicle.

ne-3c25db81.stem: After a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia, the baby's arm lies adducted and internally rotated at the side, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated (the 'waiter's tip' position). Which structure is affected?
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) – Klumpke palsy
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6) – Erb–Duchenne palsy
ne-3c25db81.explanation: Forcibly widening the angle between head and shoulder stretches the upper trunk. Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus (abduction and external rotation), biceps and brachialis (elbow flexion) and the supinators are paralysed, and the arm takes up the typical position.

ne-7352de71.stem: A patient who grabbed a branch while falling, so that the arm was forcibly pulled upwards, develops clawing of the hand, wasting of the intrinsic muscles, sensory loss on the inner forearm, and ptosis with miosis on the same side. What is the lesion?
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) – Klumpke palsy
Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5–C6)
Injury of the radial nerve in the axilla
Injury of the median nerve at the wrist
ne-7352de71.explanation: Forcible traction of the abducted arm stretches the lower trunk (C8–T1): the intrinsic muscles of the hand are paralysed and a claw hand develops. Involvement of the sympathetic fibres near the T1 root (stellate ganglion) explains the Horner syndrome.

ne-abc65d94.stem: Which of the following nerves does NOT arise from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?
ne-abc65d94.explanation: The posterior cord gives the branches supplying the back of the shoulder and arm: the upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves. The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord and supplies the anterior compartment of the arm.

ne-b856c3f9.stem: From which parts of the brachial plexus is the median nerve formed?
ne-b856c3f9.explanation: The median nerve is formed by two roots from the lateral and medial cords that join in front of the axillary artery (C6–T1, sometimes with C5 fibres). It gives no branches in the arm; it supplies most of the forearm flexors and the thenar muscles.

ne-cd2e97f1.stem: Which nerves give no branches at all in the arm (brachium)?
ne-cd2e97f1.explanation: Although the median and ulnar nerves run through the arm, they give no motor or sensory branches there; their branches are in the forearm and hand. The anterior compartment of the arm is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve and the posterior compartment by the radial nerve.

ne-cfd5de8f.stem: Which of the following dermatome pairings is wrong?
options: S1 – lateral edge of the foot and heel
ne-cfd5de8f.explanation: In the hand the thumb is C6, the middle finger C7 and the little finger C8. On the trunk T4 is the nipple, T10 the umbilicus and L1 the groin; on the leg L4 is the medial malleolus, L5 the dorsum of the foot and big toe, and S1 the lateral edge of the foot and the heel.

ne-78ef009f.stem: An obese patient who wears a tight belt has burning, numbness and tingling over the anterolateral thigh; muscle power and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is compressed?
ne-78ef009f.explanation: Meralgia paraesthetica: the purely sensory lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3) is compressed as it passes under the inguinal ligament just medial to the ASIS. Because it has no motor fibres, there is no weakness.

ne-4b8d4357.stem: Which of the following is NOT expected after a femoral nerve injury?
options: Sensory loss on the front of the thigh
Sensory loss on the medial side of the leg
ne-4b8d4357.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) supplies quadriceps, sartorius, iliacus and pectineus, and carries sensation from the front of the thigh and, through the saphenous nerve, from the medial side of the leg. The adductors are supplied by the obturator nerve.

ne-1b1b302a.stem: After prolonged pelvic surgery a patient has difficulty bringing the legs together and numbness over a small area on the inner thigh. Which nerve was injured?
ne-1b1b302a.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2–L4) runs on the lateral pelvic wall, near the ovarian fossa, and enters the obturator canal. It can be injured in pelvic surgery, by tumours or in difficult labour; the thigh adductors weaken and sensation is lost on the inner thigh.

ne-96063403.stem: At what level does the sciatic nerve most often divide into its two terminal branches (tibial and common fibular nerves)?
options: As it leaves the greater sciatic foramen
At the very top of the thigh, at the gluteal fold
At the neck of the fibula
At the upper angle of the popliteal fossa
ne-96063403.explanation: The sciatic nerve (L4–S3), the thickest nerve in the body, usually divides at the apex of the popliteal fossa. Sometimes the division is higher and the fibular part pierces piriformis.

ne-7800f94a.stem: Which of the following results from injury to the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa?
options: Foot drop and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot
Sensory loss on the medial side of the leg
Loss of plantar flexion of the foot and of toe flexion, sensory loss on the sole
Loss of eversion of the foot
ne-7800f94a.explanation: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment muscles (triceps surae, tibialis posterior, long flexors) and, through its plantar branches, the muscles of the sole. After injury the foot is held in dorsiflexion and eversion (calcaneovalgus), the patient cannot walk on tiptoe and sensation on the sole is lost.

ne-bbd6023c.stem: Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
ne-bbd6023c.explanation: The voluntarily controlled external anal and external urethral sphincters are supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4). The internal sphincters are smooth muscle and are controlled by autonomic nerves.

ne-91182414.stem: The spinal (dorsal root) ganglion contains the cell bodies of which cells?
ne-91182414.explanation: The peripheral process of the pseudounipolar neurons in the dorsal root ganglion receives information from receptors, and the central process enters the spinal cord in the dorsal root. There are no synapses in this ganglion. The herpes zoster virus lies latent here.
